_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss (Helen's failed tests vs Marcus's change of method; Marcus's job vs Helen's husband as the reason to learn; Priya's nerves vs Helen's three attempts; Helen's coast drive vs Marcus's journey home from work; Helen's daughter vs Priya's son). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 8.
title: Behind the wheel at last
subtitle: Four people describe learning to drive long after most of their friends.

sections.A: Helen, 58, librarian. For thirty years my husband did all the driving, and I was perfectly happy in the passenger seat with a map I never actually needed to read. Then he hurt his back badly, and for six months he couldn't drive at all. Suddenly someone had to take him to his hospital appointments, and that someone was me. My instructor was a cheerful young man, younger than my own daughter, who called every roundabout 'a little adventure'. I failed my first test for going too slowly and my second for going too fast, which I thought showed real progress. I passed the third time. My husband has fully recovered now, but I haven't given the keys back. Last month I drove to the coast on my own, just because I could, and sang all the way there.
sections.B: Marcus, 34, nurse. I grew up in the middle of a big city, where a car was more trouble than it was worth, so I never bothered. Then I got a job at a hospital twenty miles out of town, working nights, and discovered that the last bus left at ten. I booked an intensive course: forty hours of lessons in a single week, with the test on the Friday. It was a disaster. By Wednesday I was so tired that I drove the wrong way round a supermarket car park, and I cancelled the test. After that I took one lesson a week, which suited me far better, and passed four months later. Now the drive home after a night shift is twenty quiet minutes that I genuinely look forward to, which is more than I could ever say for the bus.
sections.C: Priya, 41, accountant. When I was nine, the car my uncle was driving slid off an icy road. Nobody was badly hurt, but for years afterwards I couldn't even sit in the front seat. At work I told everyone I took the train because I liked having time to read, and I don't think anyone ever suspected. What finally got me started was my son turning seventeen. He was booking lessons, and he said, half joking, that we could learn together. So we did, with the same instructor, on alternate days. He was far better at it than me and very patient about it, which was rather humbling. I passed first time, although I was shaking so much that the examiner offered me a glass of water. Even now, I'll take the long way round rather than go on the motorway.
sections.D: Graham, 63, retired postman. I delivered letters by bike for forty years, and when I retired, my wife suggested I take up something relaxing, like gardening. Instead I booked driving lessons. There was no real reason; I'd always wondered what it would be like, and I didn't want to reach seventy still wondering. I loved it from the first lesson, even the reversing, which I'm told is unusual. My wife, who has been driving since she was eighteen, says I drive exactly the way I used to deliver the post: slowly, carefully and looking at every front garden. She isn't entirely wrong. We bought a small second-hand car last spring, and on Sundays we drive out to villages I used to cycle through while I point out which houses had the friendliest dogs.

questions.question: Which person changed the way they were learning after a difficult start?
questions.why: 'It was a disaster… After that I took one lesson a week, which suited me far better.' Helen also had setbacks, but she failed tests rather than changing how she learned.

questions.question: Which person has had their driving compared to the way they used to work?
questions.why: His wife says 'I drive exactly the way I used to deliver the post'. Helen's examiners commented on her speed, but not in relation to her job.

questions.question: Which person started learning because someone else was suddenly unable to drive?
questions.why: Her husband 'hurt his back badly… couldn't drive at all', so 'that someone was me'. Marcus also had to learn, but because of a new job, not another person.

questions.question: Which person gave other people a false reason for not driving?
questions.why: 'I told everyone I took the train because I liked having time to read', hiding her fear after the accident.

questions.question: Which person needed more than one attempt to pass the driving test?
questions.why: She failed twice and 'passed the third time'. Priya was shaking but passed first time; Marcus cancelled his first test rather than failing it.

questions.question: Which person learned out of curiosity rather than necessity?
questions.why: 'There was no real reason; I'd always wondered what it would be like.' Helen and Marcus both learned because they had to.

questions.question: Which person learned to drive alongside a relative?
questions.why: She and her son learned 'together… with the same instructor, on alternate days'. Helen mentions her daughter only to show how young her instructor was.

questions.question: Which person now enjoys a journey connected with their work?
questions.why: 'The drive home after a night shift is twenty quiet minutes that I genuinely look forward to.' Helen enjoys her drive to the coast, but it has nothing to do with work.

questions.question: Which person has kept driving after the original reason for learning disappeared?
questions.why: 'My husband has fully recovered now, but I haven't given the keys back.'

questions.question: Which person still avoids a particular kind of road?
questions.why: 'I'll take the long way round rather than go on the motorway.'
